clinicalPearls: HIV is a retrovirus whose hallmark is progressive depletion of CD4+ T lymphocytes; the resulting immunodeficiency underlies the susceptibility to opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556).

Consider acute (primary) HIV infection in a patient presenting with a mononucleosis-like illness: sore throat is reported by roughly half of patients with acute HIV infection, often together with fever, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia and rash (p.1556; cross-ref ch.38 p.293).

The acute retroviral syndrome rash is typically a nonspecific diffuse macular/papular eruption favouring the upper thorax, face and collar region; less commonly urticarial or vesicular lesions occur, and oral or genital ulcers may accompany it (p.1556; cross-ref Appendix A1).
After primary infection there is HIV seroconversion, then a usually asymptomatic phase, and ultimately progression to symptomatic HIV disease/AIDS if untreated (cross-ref ch.38 p.297).

Three diagnostic markers appear sequentially in primary infection: HIV viral load (RNA) first, then p24 antigen, then HIV antibody; modern fourth-generation Ag/Ab combination assays shorten the window period by detecting p24 antigen before antibody is present (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1).

The CD4+ T-cell count stratifies opportunistic-infection risk: as the count falls (notably below ~200 cells/uL) the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex and CMV end-organ disease rises, guiding prophylaxis decisions (p.1556; cross-ref ch.62, ch.108).

A nondetectable (suppressed) HIV viral load on antiretroviral therapy is the goal of treatment; sustained viral suppression is the basis of the Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) principle and of treatment-as-prevention (cross-ref ch.108 p.745).

Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for essentially all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count; in patients with concurrent malignancy or other illness, ART should run concurrently with the primary treatment together with appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis (cross-ref ch.108 p.745).
Doses and specific drug regimens are deliberately omitted here; ART is presented only as a principle (combination antiretroviral therapy to achieve durable viral suppression).
harrison.pathophysiology: HIV is a human retrovirus that infects cells bearing the CD4 receptor together with a chemokine co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), leading to progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4+ T lymphocytes (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556; co-receptor role cross-ref ch.61 p.448, ch.63). Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome, establishing lifelong infection and a latent reservoir. Primary infection produces a burst of high-level viremia (the acute retroviral syndrome) followed by partial immune control and a viral set point, then a prolonged clinically latent phase during which CD4+ T cells are gradually lost. Once CD4+ T-cell counts fall sufficiently, the profound cellular immunodeficiency permits opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses. The mononuclear phagocyte system can also be infected and serves as a reservoir (cross-ref ch.63 p.461).
additionalDifferentials: Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) and acute CMV infection (overlapping mononucleosis-like picture; cross-ref Appendix A1)
Acute viral exanthems and other causes of fever with rash (e.g., secondary syphilis, enteroviral exanthem)
Streptococcal/viral pharyngitis when sore throat predominates in acute HIV (cross-ref ch.38 p.293)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug hypersensitivity reaction with fever and morbilliform rash
Autoinflammatory/connective-tissue disease presenting with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy
additionalInvestigations: Fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay with supplemental confirmatory antibody differentiation assay (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1)
HIV RNA (plasma viral load) quantification — diagnostic in the early window before antibody, and the key on-treatment monitoring test (cross-ref ch.126; ch.108)
CD4+ T-lymphocyte count to stage immunodeficiency and guide opportunistic-infection prophylaxis
HIV genotypic resistance testing recommended before starting antiretrovirals (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1)
Screening for co-infections (hepatitis B, hepatitis C) prior to immunosuppressive or antineoplastic therapy in HIV-positive patients (cross-ref ch.108 p.745)
redFlags: New CD4+ count below ~200 cells/uL — high risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia and other opportunistic infections; prompts prophylaxis (cross-ref ch.62 p.461)

Clinical or radiographic worsening after starting ART suggesting immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), especially with an underlying opportunistic infection such as PML (cross-ref ch.205 p.1490)
Features suggesting an AIDS-defining opportunistic process (e.g., focal neurologic deficit from toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma; cross-ref ch.30)

Adrenal insufficiency precipitated by stress or steroidogenesis-inhibiting drugs in advanced HIV — adrenal involvement is usually subclinical but can become clinically significant (cross-ref ch.49 p.379)
harrison.prognosis: Untreated HIV infection is progressive and ultimately fatal once advanced immunodeficiency and AIDS-defining illnesses supervene. Effective antiretroviral therapy that achieves a durable nondetectable viral load markedly improves survival and restores immune function; for example, in HIV-positive patients with PML, institution of ART enhances survival, and those with higher CD4 counts (>300/uL) and low or nondetectable HIV viral loads have a better prognosis (cross-ref ch.205, p.1490).
pitfalls: Failing to consider acute HIV in a mononucleosis-like illness: although about half of patients with acute HIV infection have a sore throat, in most U.S. settings only about 1% of patients with viral or mononucleosis-like symptoms actually have acute HIV — a negative antibody test early does not exclude it, so check viral load/p24 (cross-ref ch.38 p.293).

Relying on antibody testing alone during the window period can miss acute infection before seroconversion; the dashed limit-of-detection and marker sequence (VL, then p24, then Ab) explain false-negative antibody results (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1).
Attributing post-ART clinical deterioration to treatment failure rather than recognising IRIS, particularly in patients with a treated or unmasked opportunistic infection (cross-ref ch.205 p.1490).
Overlooking subclinical adrenal insufficiency in advanced HIV, which may be unmasked by stress or by drugs that inhibit steroidogenesis (cross-ref ch.49 p.379).
harrison.severityClassification: Staging is based on the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count, which predicts the spectrum of opportunistic disease: relatively preserved counts carry low opportunistic-infection risk, whereas progressively lower counts (notably <200 cells/uL) define increasing risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex and CMV disease, with the lowest counts associated with the broadest range of AIDS-defining illnesses (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556; opportunistic-infection associations cross-ref ch.62, ch.222, ch.227, ch.235).
